notable_claims: The University of Nebraska's removal of alt.* newsgroups was debated as either an economic necessity or a form of censorship.
Iowa State University's ethics policy was criticized for prohibiting rude expression and political speech, which some argued violated academic freedom.
Cornell University counsel claimed the ECPA of 1986 did not apply to its email services because they were provided only to the Cornell community rather than the public.
organizations: Nebraska University Students for Electronic Freedom
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several disputes regarding computer use policies at universities, including the removal of alt.* newsgroups at the University of Nebraska and speech restrictions at Iowa State University. It also addresses legal and ethical debates over email privacy, postmaster access to messages, and the applicability of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) in university settings. The item highlights the tension between institutional resource management and academic freedom.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.16

notable_claims: Unauthorized access to files, usernames, or passwords is considered a violation of university policy
Obscene or offensive material is prohibited from being entered into the computer system
Commercial use of university systems requires written authorization from the Director of the Computer Center
classification.summary: The item presents the official computer usage policy for North Dakota State University. It outlines prohibitions against unauthorized access to files, system degradation, obscene material, and copyright infringement. The policy specifies that violations are subject to student disciplinary procedures or employment sanctions.
classification.title: NDSU Policy on Misuse of Computer Facilities

notable_claims: Censorship may be masquerading as cost-saving in the removal of alt.* newsgroups.
The benefit per dollar of Usenet access is high compared to other information sources.
classification.summary: Lee Story responds to a discussion regarding the University of Nebraska's decision to remove the alt.* Usenet hierarchy. Story argues that cost-saving justifications for removing these groups are often masks for censorship and suggests students would likely pay small fees to maintain access.
classification.title: Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

identity.subject: Article 2--Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

notable_claims: Institutions are not obligated to provide a full news feed, but refusing student-funded hardware for that purpose may be a free speech issue.
Running a campus-wide Usenet feed for thousands of users requires significant investment in administration and hardware beyond just a basic machine.
The cost of setting up a dedicated news machine at a large institution can exceed $10,000.
classification.summary: Peter Deutsch discusses the tension between institutional funding and free speech regarding the removal of the alt.* Usenet hierarchy at the University of Nebraska. He argues that while institutions aren't obligated to fund news feeds, preventing students from self-funding their own access would constitute a free speech issue. He shares his personal experience managing an unsponsored Internet link at McGill University to illustrate the administrative and financial burdens of providing campus-wide access.
classification.title: Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

identity.subject: Article 3--Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

notable_claims: Filtering newsgroups based on technical noise or size is a standard function of hierarchies.
Removing groups specifically to control content (e.g., removing rec.humor for being 'racist') constitutes censorship.
classification.summary: Brad Templeton discusses the ethics and practicalities of Usenet newsgroup filtering at universities, specifically regarding the University of Nebraska's removal of 'alt.*' groups. He argues that removing large or noisy hierarchies for technical reasons is acceptable, whereas removals based on content control (censorship) are legitimate targets for protest.
classification.title: Article 4--Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

identity.subject: Article 4--Re: news story on U. of Nebraska alt.* removal

notable_claims: NUSEF sought to extend First Amendment rights specifically to computer and network systems.
The group positioned itself as a watchdog against university administration and the CRC.
organizations: Nebraska University Students for Electronic Freedom
classification.summary: The Nebraska University Students for Electronic Freedom (NUSEF) adopted a Statement of Purpose to promote academic freedom and First Amendment rights on university computer systems. The group aimed to act as a watchdog over the Computing Resource Center (CRC) regarding privacy and administrative policies. Their goals included educating the community on electronic freedoms and broadening access to communication systems.
classification.title: Statement of Purpose: Nebraska University Students for Electronic Freedom

identity.subject: Article 5--Re: An Open Letter to UNL CRC: Removal of alt.*

notable_claims: Under USC 18, service providers have the right to view mail in the course of providing communication services.
University officials charged with academic discipline may be considered 'law enforcement' for the purpose of divulging communications.
Owlnet policy explicitly warns users that no computer security system can absolutely prevent unauthorized access and that administrators can bypass file permissions.
classification.summary: Joseph A. Watters discusses the legal and ethical implications of email monitoring in U.S. academic environments, citing USC 18 regarding electronic communications. He provides examples of Rice University's Owlnet policies, which explicitly state that system administrators may access user files and emails for operational integrity or official university investigations into misconduct.
classification.title: Article 6--Re: EMAIL PRIVACY

notable_claims: System administrators should not restrict their own ability to access any data on their machines.
Technical necessity (e.g., debugging mail headers in VMS) justifies the administrative ability to view message bodies.
classification.summary: Leonard J. Schmidt argues that system administrators and postmasters should maintain the technical ability to access email bodies for debugging and system management purposes. He distinguishes between the ability to see a message body and the ability to understand its meaning, noting that encryption is an acceptable way for users to protect content. He cites specific technical limitations of DEC Vax/VMS systems where headers often appear in the message body as a practical justification for admin access.
classification.title: Article 7--RE: EMAIL PRIVACY (a side note)

notable_claims: It is generally not a crime or civil tort for a recipient to publish a private communication they received.
The author of a letter holds a 'common law copyright' in the exact expression, but this does not preclude fair use publication.
Quoting an administrator's email to protest unauthorized directory examination is considered protected fair use.
classification.summary: Professor Peter D. Junger disputes a claim that publishing private emails without the sender's consent is illegal. He argues that recipients generally have the right to publish communications they receive and that quoting such messages to protest system administrator surveillance constitutes fair use.
classification.title: Article 8--Legality of quoting letters

notable_claims: Cornell's CIT used a program called 'sys$manager:spy' to track a student's logins without notification.
Cornell counsel argued that the ECPA of 1986 does not apply because they do not provide email services 'to the public'.
CIT administration claimed email is not private and should be treated as potentially public information.
classification.summary: Peter Wayner reports on a dispute at Cornell University involving the monitoring of a student's computer activity by Communications and Information Technologies (CIT). The incident involved the use of a program called 'sys$manager:spy' to notify administrators of a specific user's logins during an investigation into the MBDF virus. The discussion highlights conflicting views on email privacy and whether the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) applies to university networks.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: News from Cornell...

notable_claims: Prohibiting rude expression or messages of a political nature on university computers violates academic freedom and the law.
Vague speech restrictions in university computer policies are consistently overturned by courts.
The UWM Post v. University of Wisconsin decision specifically addresses protected offensive expression via email.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie critiques a computer ethics policy at Iowa State University, arguing that its restrictions on 'rude' and 'political' expression violate academic freedom and the First Amendment. He advocates for wider user participation in policy formulation and references legal precedents regarding offensive expression via email. The post emphasizes that vague speech restrictions are often overturned by courts.
classification.title: Re: [info.labmgr] Ethics statement

notable_claims: Iowa State University restricted newsgroups related to sex and drugs but allowed access via a request form.
The author argues that maintaining lists of users requesting restricted content is not a significant privacy violation compared to other commercial or library records.
The debate highlights a tension between the 'anarchical nature' of Usenet and the administrative desire to police offensive or illegal content in academic settings.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding a new policy at Iowa State University that restricted access to Usenet newsgroups dealing with sex and drugs. The author, Michael Nolan, compares this approach to a more restrictive policy at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, arguing that ISU's model of 'informed consent' via request forms is preferable to outright censorship.
classification.title: USENET Censorship at Iowa State University

identity.subject: Article 11--Re: USENET Censorship at Iowa State University

notable_claims: The Newsletter on Intellectual Freedom only prints reports documented with newspaper articles.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie encourages the reporting of computer-media and academic computer censorship to the American Library Association's Newsletter on Intellectual Freedom. He notes that the newsletter requires documentation via newspaper articles for reports to be printed. Kadie also requests copies of news articles regarding censorship on academic computers for his own records.
classification.title: Publicizing computer-media censorship
